content:
Dozens of presidential briefing documents were declassified on Friday, marking the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks, detailing intelligence gathered by government officials about Osama bin Laden and al-Qaeda before the hijackings. The attacks killed nearly 3,000 people and fundamentally reshaped America's national security landscape.

The documents reveal how security analysts tracked bin Laden's movements and support network, as well as concerns about potential threats to US targets. They also detail officials' understanding of his networks in the United States and other countries, including how his operations were funded.

CIA Director John Ratcliffe described the move as an "act of extraordinary transparency," saying the documents represent the largest single declassification of Presidential Daily Briefs by the CIA. The President's Daily Brief is prepared by the intelligence community for the government's top leadership and is highly classified.

The documents span a wide range, with the earliest dating to a February 1998 file prepared for then-President Bill Clinton titled "Terrorists Seek Weapons of Mass Destruction," which mentioned bin Laden and other Islamic extremists; the latest is a September 12, 2001 report in which a source noted the attacks had been planned for two years and had included the US Capitol as a target.

An April 1998 document described the Taliban's reluctance to hand over bin Laden, viewing him at the time in Afghanistan as merely a "guest" of the Taliban, and noted the Taliban "appreciated his assistance during the Soviet occupation" and thus "did not wish to offend him by monitoring or restricting his activities."

Briefers in July 1998 assessed that "bin Laden is likely to prioritize striking the US on his list," and noted his "interest in using chemical and biological weapons to carry out attacks."

Two months later, a briefer wrote that bin Laden's "preferred method is to launch an attack on the US homeland in Washington," and noted that al-Qaeda "might pilot an explosives-laden aircraft into a US city."

The possibility of hijackings was also raised in December 1998, when a briefer described accomplices "having recently conducted test runs at an undisclosed airport in New York without being stopped by security," and noted that "members of the bin Laden network have received hijacking training."

Other documents detail how bin Laden sought materials to build a "dirty bomb" — a conventional weapon laced with radioactive material. Intelligence officials said that by June 1999, his operatives had conducted related explosive experiments to "enhance the destructive power of the blast."

About two years before the attacks, intelligence officials noticed that bin Laden appeared to be concealing from the Taliban his intentions to launch unprovoked strikes against the United States. Briefings prepared in early 2001 for President George W. Bush focused in part on bin Laden "crudely experimenting with manufacturing and deploying biological weapons."

A report one month before the attacks stated that bin Laden was "determined to strike within the United States," and referenced the 1998 al-Qaeda bombings of US embassies as showing "he will spend years preparing an operation and will not be deterred by setbacks."

By August 2001, officials wrote in a report that "there are suspicious activities in the United States consistent with preparations for hijackings or other types of attacks, including recent surveillance of federal buildings in New York," and added that the FBI was "conducting approximately 70 full-field investigations related to bin Laden throughout the United States."

Many of the documents were redacted to conceal the identities of sources and other identifying information. The documents do not appear to offer new breakthroughs regarding the planning of the attacks or US officials' understanding of events as they unfolded.

In the years after the attacks, a bipartisan commission specifically highlighted the lack of intelligence sharing between agencies such as the CIA and FBI, and issued recommendations that led to the creation of new positions, including the Director of National Intelligence and the National Counterterrorism Center, which analyzes terrorism-related information from across the government domestically and abroad.

When asked about the declassified documents, the White House noted that the National Archives also declassified another set of documents on Friday. That batch includes interview transcripts with national security officials from the Clinton and Bush administrations, produced by a commission that investigated the attacks between 2002 and 2004.
